sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

The checklist turned up no `no` answers. I'm adding one finding that the checklist has no line for (copy).

1. *(Not a checklist line. It comes from the copy check: "copy that could sit on anyone's page".)* The headline "The finest bread in the valley" (about x 110–1085, y 185–415) is the biggest and most dominant thing on the page. It is also the most generic line on it. Almost any bakery could say it, and it asks the viewer to take a superlative on trust. Everything that actually sets this bakery apart is in the 20 px subline at y 450–500 and the kicker at y 132: "since 1962", "wood-fired oven", "every morning", "Mill Street". So the eye lands first on the line that says least. Only a reader who goes on to the small text learns why this bakery is different. **Fix:** move one of those specific claims into the headline so the dominant line carries the proof, for example the wood-fired oven or baking every morning since 1962. Then let the subline add the rest. **Taste**, argued on its own terms. **Weight:** major, because it is the element the page leads with.

**What's working.**
- **One mood throughout.** A warm cream ground, a classical text serif at display size, a small tracked sans kicker in a bread-crust brown, and dark charcoal text all share the same calm, traditional, crafted feel. Nothing reads as borrowed from another era, so the page reads as one piece and suits an old local bakery.
- **No excess.** There are no rules, boxes, badges or ornaments. Every element on the page has a job: who (kicker), the claim (headline), and the proof (subline). Removing any one of them would lose something.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** This looks like the top of a homepage that has no picture of the bread and no next step: no hours, no order or visit link, and the bottom 300 px is empty. I can't tell whether that comes later in the scroll or below the fold. If it doesn't, the hierarchy and interface critics should check it.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
Walk (working notes):

First read: the eye lands on the big serif headline "The finest bread in the valley", moves up to the small brown "HARTLEY'S BAKERY · SINCE 1962", then down to the two-line sans description. It reads as the hero of a local bakery's homepage: warm, calm and traditional. The job is my assumption: a small bakery's landing hero that says who they are and what they bake.

What matters first:
- One element dominates: **yes**. The headline (cap height about 90 px, y≈185–415) is far bigger than anything else.
- Each text level distinct at a glance: **yes**. There are three levels: the eyebrow (about 14 px, tracked caps, bold, brown), the headline (about 110 px serif) and the body (about 20 px sans, dark). The eyebrow and body are close in size, but caps, weight and colour separate them.
- Headings differ by more than size: **yes**. The serif headline sits against the sans body and eyebrow.

All lines are yes, so there were no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headline clearly dominates.** It is set at about 110 px, roughly five times the 20 px body, in near-black serif (x 110–1085, y≈185–415). The eye has one obvious place to start, and the step down to the body is too big to misread. Keep that ratio.
- **The smaller levels are told apart by more than size.** The eyebrow (y≈132) is about 14 px, in bold tracked caps and warm brown, so it reads as a label above the headline. The body is plain dark sans at about 20 px. They are close in size but never collide, because caps, weight and colour do the separating (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger).

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: this section applies. The image is a one-column hero with an eyebrow, a two-line serif headline and a subline, all set flush left at x≈110 on a 1280×800 frame. The crop script was refused because Bash is denied, so I judged from the whole image. At this size that loses nothing.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No.
   - **Where:** All the content sits in the top-left, from x 110 to 1085 and y 120 to 500. The heaviest mass is the dark headline at y 185–415. The block's centre is at about y 310, against a frame centre of 400. The top margin is about 120 px, while the bottom 300 px (y 500–800) is empty across the full width. Right of the subline, x 720–1280 is also empty.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The frame looks top-heavy and unfinished. The eye finishes the subline and drops into an empty band with nothing to settle on, so the lower part reads as a missing button, picture or next section rather than chosen space.
   - **Why:** Visual weight comes from size, darkness and isolation, and a heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Here the dark headline mass has nothing to counter it below or to the right.
   - **What would make it fine:** If the live page has a call to action, an image, or the top of the next section showing in this band, this is not a defect. The capture shows none of these.
   - **Direction of the fix:** Either give the lower band a counterweight, such as a call to action or a picture of the bread, or bring the block down until the space above and below reads as intended. Another option is to shorten the frame so the empty area belongs to the composition.
   - **Kind:** Convention (Arnheim), with the degree a matter of taste.
   - **Weight:** Minor.

**What's working.**
- **One strong left edge.** The eyebrow, the headline's "T" and "v", and the subline all hang from the same x≈110 line, optically exact. That single edge holds the stack together and shows the asymmetry is on purpose. Keep it when adding anything below.
- **Space gathered in one place.** The empty space is one large L-shaped area rather than small gaps spread around, which gives the dense headline room and keeps the page calm. The spacing between eyebrow, headline and subline (about 50 px and 45 px) also keeps them reading as one block.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether this is a cropped viewport with the next section or a call to action just below the fold. That decides whether finding 1 stands.
- How the flush-left block and the headline line break behave on narrower screens.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances).

sections.report:
I found one real problem in the text: the headline puts "valley" alone on its second line. The rest of the type is in good shape.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line?** and **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries?** The headline breaks after "in the", leaving "valley" alone on line 2 (about x 110–350, y 320–410). The two lines are badly unbalanced: line 1 runs to about x 1085 and line 2 stops at about x 350. "the valley" is one phrase, so the reader stops on the article "the" at the end of line 1 before reaching the noun. The word that carries the claim, "valley", ends up as a short leftover word in the space where the headline should hold together. Bringhurst 2.4.2 covers the lone short word on a last line. The point about phrase breaks in headings has no confirmed source, so treat that part as common sense. Fix: balance the two lines and break at the phrase, for example "The finest bread / in the valley". That means a manual break, `text-wrap: balance`, or a narrower headline measure, and it should hold at every viewport width. Defect (mild). Weight: minor. The headline still reads, but it is the most visible text on the page and right now it looks unfinished.
2. **Are quotation marks curly, and are dashes and ellipses the true characters?** The apostrophe in "HARTLEY'S" in the eyebrow (about x 175, y 132) looks like a straight typewriter mark, not a curly one (’). At 15 px in caps it is barely visible. Fix: use a real ’ in the source. No confirmed source covers curly quotes, so this is taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The type plan is clear. A refined, old-style serif headline sits over a plain sans for the subhead and eyebrow: two faces that are obviously different, each with its own job. The serif gives the warmth and tradition a 1962 bakery wants, and the sans keeps the practical details easy to read.
- The subhead is set well: about 20 px, about 55 characters per line, comfortable line spacing, flush left, dark on cream. The headline's "fi" is properly joined as a ligature, and the caps in the eyebrow are letterspaced. The details are looked after.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 27 yes, 3 no (paragraphs and columns break cleanly; headings break at phrase boundaries; curly quotes and true dashes), 0 unsure

**First read.** The eye lands on the large serif headline, reads down to the sans body text, and only then takes in the small brown line above. It reads as the top of a bakery's home page: warm, quiet and traditional. Colour plays a supporting role here and keeps out of the way.

**Checklist walk (colour)**
- Small palette: yes. There is a warm cream background, near-black text and one brown accent.
- Strong colour kept to a small share of the area: yes. The only saturated colour is the brown eyebrow, which takes up a tiny area.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on a pale ground holds up in grayscale.
- Warm colours on what comes forward: yes. The warm brown marks the brand line. The cream ground is warm but very low in saturation, so it sits back.
- Colours meant to match look the same: yes. The headline and body share the same near-black and look identical.
- Neighbouring strong colours differ in lightness: yes. There are no strong colours next to each other.
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not shown by colour alone: yes. The colour carries no meaning on its own.
- Dark theme not pure black: yes. This is a light theme, so the line doesn't apply.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so I didn't need to open any entries. The Bash tool was refused, so I didn't run the crop script. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

---

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The palette fits a bakery.** The warm off-white ground (roughly #FAF6EF by eye) and the bread-crust brown of the eyebrow "HARTLEY'S BAKERY · SINCE 1962" (x≈110–410, y≈124–140) give an old, homely warmth without photos. It uses one neutral range and one hue, which suits the brand.
- **Colour and value are in proportion.** Near-black (not pure black) text on cream gives strong but soft contrast for the headline and body. The brown accent is limited to one short line, so it marks the brand and the date without competing with the headline. That matches the "accent color restraint" line of the colour checklist.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
